insider_note: This substitution — split off sec²θ, then put tanθ=y — is the standard method for any even power of secθ or cosecθ.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Split off sec²θ and substitute tanθ=y
steps.margin_note: First mark. sec⁴θ = sec²θ·sec²θ = sec²θ(1+tan²θ) — always split off one sec²θ as the dy piece.
steps.memory_tip: Any even power of secθ splits as sec²θ(1+tan²θ)^k — the substitution tanθ=y always works.
lines: Put tanθ = y ⇒ sec²θ dθ = dy
steps.why: Splitting off one factor of sec²θ as the derivative of tanθ turns sec⁴θ into sec²θ(1+tan²θ), a form ready for the substitution tanθ=y, since sec²θdθ is exactly dy.
common_mistakes: Trying to integrate sec⁴θ directly by a standard sec formula that does not exist.
Forgetting to convert the limits from θ to y after substituting.

steps.label: Integrate and apply the limits
steps.margin_note: Second mark. 1 + 1/3 = 4/3 — a straightforward final addition.
steps.memory_tip: The upper limit y=1 makes every term in y+y³/3 equal to its own coefficient, since 1ⁿ=1 for any n.
steps.why: Integrating the polynomial 1+y² term by term gives y+y³/3, and substituting y=1 (the upper limit) and y=0 (the lower limit, contributing nothing) gives 1+1/3.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the y³/3 term and reporting the answer as just 1.
